SK3020 The non-async Task method returns null

A method whose declared return type is Task or Task<T> and which is not async returns null or default.

CategoryAsync
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS4586

Why

A Task return type invites the caller to write await Something(), and awaiting null is a NullReferenceException whose stack names the caller rather than the method that produced it. An async method cannot do this — the compiler wraps whatever it returns — so the shape exists only where the signature was written by hand, and there return null; looks exactly like every other "nothing to do" in the file. Task.CompletedTask is the completed task the caller was promised.

Example

Instead of:

Task Flush(bool dirty) {
    if (!dirty) {
        return null;
    }

    return writer.FlushAsync();
}

Write:

Task Flush(bool dirty) {
    if (!dirty) {
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    return writer.FlushAsync();
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The fix is unsafe by declaration and the generic form is why. Task.CompletedTask is the only completed non-generic task there is, so that half is mechanical; Task.FromResult<T>(default!) picks a value the method never named, and what a completed task should carry is a decision about the method rather than an edit. Applying it turns a crash into a default result, which is the point of the rule and is still a behaviour change somebody should read. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions, only where the declared return type resolves to System.Threading.Tasks.Task or Task<T>, and only for a literal null or default — a null-valued local, a conditional whose branch is null, and a default(Task) are the same bug and are not matched, because the rule reports what it can rewrite in one span. ⚠ `async` withdraws it: async Task<string> returning null returns a null string inside a real task, which is an ordinary nullable-reference question. ⚠ `Task?` withdraws it too, because the author has declared that null is a value this method returns and the contract already carries the warning. ValueTask is not covered: it is a struct and cannot be null. ⚠ The replacement is not built by editing the declaration's text — an alias (using MyTask = System.Threading.Tasks.Task;) makes the written name resolve to something a string edit would get wrong. The rule asks whether the simple name Task means System.Threading.Tasks.Task at that position and falls back to the fully qualified name, which always binds.
